title: Asking politely
job: Requests, thanks, apologies in the right register
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: LATIN HAS NO POLITE 'YOU', and this is the module where that matters. Every other language in this app gives you a second pronoun for respect — usted, vous, Sie, Lei. Latin does not: tū is one person and vōs is more than one, and vōs to a single person is not formal, it is wrong. Politeness lives in the VERB and in a handful of fixed phrases, all of which are here.

velim is the polite 'I would like', and it is softer than L1's volō. Velim aquam asks; aquam volō states. It is a subjunctive — a shape of the verb this course has not taught and will not explain here — so learn it as a word, the way you learned quantī cōnstat. There is exactly one other subjunctive in this level, and it is M6's.

quaesō is the nearest thing Latin has to 'please', and it is a verb meaning 'I ask'. It goes at the end, after a comma, and it does not change the command in front of it: Dā mihi aquam, quaesō. sīs is the other softener, worn down from sī vīs, 'if you would'.

nōlī plus an infinitive is how you tell somebody NOT to do something: Nōlī īre, 'don't go'. It is the command form of nōlō, L1-M3's one-word refusal, so it is the same verb doing a new job. It is an imperative and not a subjunctive, even though it sits next to velim in this module.

grātiās agō is 'thank you', and it is literally 'I do thanks' — L1-M2's agō with a new object. Add tibi for 'I thank YOU' when the person matters. Nothing here is new grammar; it is one verb you know and one noun you do not.

mē paenitet is 'I am sorry', and it is built the way L1-M3's mihi opus est was built: impersonally. Nobody is the subject but the regret itself, and mē is the object shape of ego — so the sentence says, roughly, 'it repents me'. English has no construction like it, which is why it has to be learned whole.

ignōsce mihi is the other apology and it is an ordinary imperative with a 'to me' after it — the same shape as L1-M8's dā mihi. Two apologies, two constructions: one is a command asking to be forgiven, the other a statement that you regret something.

words.note: The polite 'I would like' — softer than L1's volō. A subjunctive, learned here as a fixed word rather than as a form: this course explains the shape at a later level.
'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā after in, cum or opus est. Three shapes of one word.

sentences.trap: There is no polite pronoun to add. The politeness is entirely in velim — swap it for volō and the same two words become a flat demand.
sentences.sound: VE-lim A-quam. Nothing long in velim; it is two short syllables and the stress is at the front.

variations.changed: L1's blunt version, for the contrast — same request, no courtesy
a different thing asked for
and again, with a thing rather than a substance

mistake.why: A plural pronoun put in as a courtesy, on the model of French or German. vōs means more than one person and nothing else, so it cannot make a request polite — and with velim, which is already first person, it has nothing at all to attach to.

sentences.usage: Said to anyone you are asking a favour of.
sentences.mnemonic: velim is volō with its edges softened.

words.note: 'Give!' — an order to one person, like salvē and valē. Its ā is long, and it takes two things after it: a 'to me' and an object.
'I' has more than one shape: ego does the acting, mihi is 'to me / for me'. The person something is given TO takes this shape.
'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā after in, cum or opus est. Three shapes of one word.
The nearest Latin has to 'please', and it is a verb: 'I ask'. It goes at the end after a comma and changes nothing about the command in front of it.

sentences.trap: quaesō is a whole verb bolted on, not a particle. English 'please' is a word that has forgotten it was ever 'if it pleases you'; quaesō has not forgotten, which is why it takes a comma.
sentences.sound: DA MI-hi A-quam, QUAE-sō. The ae of quaesō is the 'eye' of English and its ō is long: KWIGH-soh.

variations.changed: a different thing asked for
the courtesy dropped, which leaves a bare order
the courtesy in front instead, which is allowed and slightly more insistent

mistake.why: 'Please' built out of placet, on the strength of the English word's history. placet is L1-M1's verb of liking and means 'it is pleasing'; dropped in here it says something closer to 'give me water, it pleases'.

sentences.mnemonic: quaesō is 'I ask' — a verb, so it gets a comma.

words.note: 'Do not!' — the command form of L1-M3's nōlō, and it takes an infinitive after it: nōlī īre. Latin forbids by telling you to be unwilling.
'I go': eō, īs 'you go', it 'he/she goes', īre 'to go'. Tiny and irregular — and the -re ending is what makes it 'to'.

sentences.trap: You cannot negate an imperative with nōn. L1-M3 said nōn goes in front of a verb, and that is true of statements only — a command needs nōlī and an infinitive, which is a different construction rather than a negated one.
sentences.sound: NO-lī I-re. Both vowels of nōlī are long and so is the ī of īre — three long vowels in four syllables makes it a slow, deliberate line.

variations.changed: a different action forbidden
the courtesy added, which softens a prohibition without changing it
the other softener, which is warmer and less formal than quaesō

mistake.why: A command negated with nōn, which is how English does it. Latin has a dedicated construction — nōlī plus the infinitive — and nōn against a bare imperative is not something a Roman wrote.

sentences.usage: Said when you need somebody to stop.

words.note: 'Thanks' — plural, always, and in the object shape because it is what you are doing. English kept it in 'gratitude' and 'grace'.
The verb agō, 'do / drive / carry on', in the shapes this level writes: agō 'I do', agis 'you do', agit 'he does', agimus 'we do'.

sentences.trap: Thanking is something you DO, and the thanks are the object. There is no word for 'you' in it at all — S05 adds one when the person matters, and this bare version is the ordinary form.
sentences.sound: GRA-ti-ās A-gō. The first ā of grātiās is long and stressed; the -ās at the end is long too but unstressed.

variations.changed: the person added, in the 'to you' shape
more than one person thanking, which is L1-M10's plural ending
a third person doing the thanking

mistake.why: The thanks left singular. Latin always thanks in the plural — grātiās — and a single grātia is 'favour' or 'charm', which turns the sentence into something closer to 'I exercise charm'.

sentences.usage: Said whenever English would say thank you.
sentences.mnemonic: Thanks are plural and they are something you DO.

words.note: 'To you' — the shape of tū that matches mihi. One person only: L1-M2's rule holds, and there is no polite plural to reach for.
'Thanks' — plural, always, and in the object shape because it is what you are doing. English kept it in 'gratitude' and 'grace'.
The verb agō, 'do / drive / carry on', in the shapes this level writes: agō 'I do', agis 'you do', agit 'he does', agimus 'we do'.

sentences.trap: tibi is the polite form and the familiar form, because there is only one. A learner who has met French or German will look for a second word here and there is none — the warmth is in adding tibi at all.
sentences.sound: TI-bi GRA-ti-ās A-gō. tibi is two short syllables, exactly like mihi, which is the pair worth hearing together.

variations.changed: more than one person thanking one person
the same three words reordered, which is allowed and very common
the person named as well as addressed

mistake.why: The object shape of tū where the 'to you' shape belongs. grātiās is already the object — a verb cannot have two — and the person thanked is who the thanks go TO, which is tibi.

sentences.usage: Said when the thanks are pointed at someone in particular.
sentences.mnemonic: mihi and tibi: to me, to you.

words.note: 'Forgive!' — an imperative with a 'to me' after it, the same shape as dā mihi. Literally 'do not take note of', from the same root as nōscō, 'I know'.
'I' has more than one shape: ego does the acting, mihi is 'to me / for me'. The person forgiven takes this shape, not the object one.

sentences.trap: You are forgiven TO rather than forgiven. The verb takes a 'to me' where English takes a plain object, which is a small thing to remember and an easy one to get wrong once dā mihi has taught the same shape for giving.
sentences.sound: ig-NOS-ce MI-hi. The ō is long and takes the stress; the c is hard, so the middle is -NOS-kay.

variations.changed: the courtesy added
somebody else forgiven, in the same 'to' shape
the 'to me' dropped and the softer word used — the casual version

mistake.why: The object shape where the 'to me' shape belongs. ignōscō governs a dative — the person is who the forgiveness goes to — so mē is wrong for the same reason it was wrong in S05.

sentences.usage: Said when you have done something small and want it overlooked.

words.note: The object shape of L1-M1's ego: ego does the acting, mē is acted on, mihi is 'to me'. Three shapes of one word, and this is the last of them.
'It repents' — impersonal, like mihi opus est. Nobody is the subject but the regret, and the person who feels it is the OBJECT: mē paenitet.

sentences.trap: You are the object of your own regret. There is no English construction like it — the nearest is the archaic 'it repenteth me' — so the two words have to be learned as a unit and not assembled.
sentences.sound: ME pae-NI-tet. The ē of mē is long; the ae of paenitet is the 'eye' sound, so it is pie-NI-tet.

variations.cue: I am sorry, please forgive me.
variations.changed: both apologies together, which is what a real apology sounds like
the person addressed, which changes nothing in the construction
negated, with nōn in front of the whole thing

mistake.why: The English subject put in the subject's chair. paenitet has no personal subject at all, so ego has nothing to be — it is L1-M1's mihi placet problem in a new construction, and the fix is the same: the person is not the subject.

sentences.usage: The real apology, as against ignōsce mihi's request.
sentences.mnemonic: It repents ME: the regret does the acting.

sentences.cue: I would like to read the book.

words.note: The polite 'I would like' — softer than L1's volō. A subjunctive, learned here as a fixed word rather than as a form: this course explains the shape at a later level.
'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one, librōs as more than one object.
'I read' AND 'I am reading' — one present for both: legō, legis, legit, legere 'to read'. The -re ending is what makes it 'to'.

sentences.trap: velim takes an infinitive exactly as volō did, and the order is the same: object, infinitive, verb. Nothing about the politeness changes the shape of the sentence — which is the useful thing about it.
sentences.sound: VE-lim LI-brum LE-ge-re. Three words, all stressed at the front, none of them long.

variations.cue: I would like to drink some water.
variations.changed: a different object and infinitive in the same frame

variations.cue: I want to read the book.
variations.changed: L1's blunt version, with the verb back at the end

variations.cue: I would like to read the book, if I may.
variations.changed: the softener added to an already polite request

mistake.why: The English order — verb, infinitive, object. Every module since L1-M3 has warned about it, and a polite sentence is exactly where a learner stops watching the order because they are concentrating on the courtesy.

sentences.usage: Said when you are asking permission as much as asking for a thing.
sentences.mnemonic: Politeness changes the verb, not the order.

words.note: 'Do not!' — the command form of L1-M3's nōlō, and it takes an infinitive after it: nōlī īre. Latin forbids by telling you to be unwilling.
'To drink', the infinitive — bibō 'I drink', bibis 'you drink', bibit 'he drinks'. The -re ending is what makes it 'to'.
The nearest Latin has to 'please', and it is a verb: 'I ask'. It goes at the end after a comma and changes nothing about the command in front of it.

sentences.trap: A prohibition can be polite without changing shape. quaesō softens it and nōlī still governs the infinitive — so the courtesy is an addition rather than an alteration, which is the pattern of the whole module.
sentences.sound: NO-lī BI-be-re, QUAE-sō. Two long vowels at the start, two short words in the middle, and the diphthong at the end.

variations.changed: the courtesy dropped

variations.cue: Please do not drink the water.
variations.changed: an object added, and it goes in front of the infinitive
a different action and the warmer softener

mistake.why: A finite verb where the infinitive belongs. nōlī governs the -re form, so bibis ('you drink') cannot follow it — the construction is 'be unwilling TO drink', and the 'to' is the ending.

sentences.usage: Said when you have to stop somebody without offending them.

sentences.cue: Pass me the bread, would you.

words.note: 'Give!' — an order to one person, like salvē and valē. Its ā is long, and it takes two things after it: a 'to me' and an object.
'I' has more than one shape: ego does the acting, mē is acted on, mihi is 'to me'. The person something is given TO takes this shape.
'Bread': pānis as the subject, pānem as the object, pāne as the thing needed. It is not a pan — the English word that kept it is 'pantry'.
'If you would' — sī vīs worn down to one syllable. Warmer and less formal than quaesō, and used between people who know each other.

sentences.trap: sīs and quaesō are not interchangeable in tone. quaesō is what you say to a stranger or a superior; sīs is what you say across a table to a friend. Neither is a grammatical choice, which is why both sit in the same module.
sentences.sound: DA MI-hi PA-nem, SIS. The ī of sīs is long, so it is SEES and not 'sis'.

variations.changed: the formal softener instead, for a stranger rather than a friend

variations.cue: Pass me the water, would you.
variations.changed: a different thing asked for

variations.cue: I would like the bread, if you would.
variations.changed: the polite request instead of the softened command — both courtesies at once

mistake.why: Not wrong at all — sī vīs is what sīs is made of, and a Roman wrote both. It is here as a plate because a learner who writes the long form has understood the word correctly and will sound bookish: sīs is what speech uses.

sentences.usage: Said at a table, to somebody you know.
sentences.mnemonic: sīs is 'if you would', squeezed into one syllable.

comprehensionPool.cue: I would like the book, please.
Pass me the book, would you.
I would like to drink some water.
